newsitem.title: UK: Brazil 97/98 sugar output may fall 10 pct - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Brazil 97/98 sugar output may fall 10 pct - analyst.

text.p: Brazilian sugar production could fall by as much as 10 percent in 1997/98 due to restructuring of the domestic market and in reaction to low world prices, an F.O. Licht analyst said on Thursday.

The debt crisis afflicting non-exporting Brazilian mills would lead to an industry consolidation which could last between three and four years, said Christoph Berg at a two-day conference hosted by Agra Europe.

"A wave of mergers and take-overs can be expected for the next two to three years, most likely starting in the third quarter of 1997 as by then the financial situation of most of the debt-ridden mills will have worsened substantially," Berg said.
"Those troubled mills which cannot find a potential partner are likely to leave the market altogether thus resulting in a further consolidation of the industry."

Those sugar mills with access to export markets, where credit costs were much lower than in Brazil, were prospering and expanding production but non-exporting mills were becoming increasingly in debt, he said.
The overall debt of the Brazilian sugar sector amounted to some $5 billion.
But after the consolidation process was complete, the overall cost structure of the remaining mills would be improved and the competitiveness of Brazilian sugar would be boosted, Berg said.
"This in turn could result in a larger share of the world market for Brazilian sugar," he said.
In its second estimate of world sugar production for 1996/97, Licht pegged Brazilian output at 14.72 million tonnes, raw value, up from 13.64 million in 1995/96.

Berg said while Brazil had an enormous potential as a low-cost sugar producer, the demands of its alcohol industry on cane availability would determine the country's future position on world sugar markets.
